newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada court bans blockades of Alaska ferries.
newsitem.headline: Canada court bans blockades of Alaska ferries.

text.p: A Canadian court on Monday granted a permanent injunction against further blockades of Alaskan ferries by Canadian fishermen angered over a dispute between Canada and the United States on salmon fishing.

Agreeing to a request from Alaska, federal Justice Barbara Reed ruled that a one-week injunction due to expire on Monday should be extended. The U.S. state said this increased the chances it will resume ferry service to Canada.
"We're very pleased. The judge has made the temporary order permanent," said Bob King, press secretary for Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles, in Vancouver after the hearing.
The judgment followed a three-day blockade of the Alaska state ferry Malaspina last week by a flotilla of 200 fishboats in Prince Rupert, about 1,000 miles (1,600 km) north of Vancouver.

The fishermen were protesting alleged overfishing of salmon by Alaska and the failure of Canada and the United States, despite years of wrangling, to agree on how to divide up this year's Pacific salmon catch.
Alaska, which says damages caused by the blockade could total more than $3 million, has denied its fishermen are overfishing.

The federal court will review the injunction when it hears arguments in a lawsuit launched by Alaska seeking to gain compensation for losses resulting from the ferry siege. That lawsuit names 200 fishermen involved in the protest and Alaska has said it will also target the Canadian government.

Canada's United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union on Monday called on British Columbia and Canada's federal government to launch countersuits seeking "millions of dollars" in damages because of reduced fish catches.

Alaska Attorney General Bruce Botelho, who was also in Vancouver for Monday's hearing, said the court ruling was a "major step" toward reinstating Prince Rupert as a stop on its ferry service between Washington state and Alaska.

But before it will return to Prince Rupert, Alaska wants assurances from the Canadian federal government that it would intervene quickly in any future blockade and to see progress in its efforts to recoup damages.
Alaska's ferry service to Prince Rupert was suspended indefinitely after the blockade despite a pledge from many of the fishermen involved that they would not repeat the action.

Gary Haydon, director of the Alaska Marine Highway System which oversees the ferry service, said the atmostphere remained too hostile to consider a resumption now. "We still have a substantial risk," he said.

Fearing further blockades, the state is taking extra precautions with a ferry due to dock at Hyder, Alaska, early Tuesday because it must travel through Canadian waters. It will carry state troopers and a Coast Guard officer on board and will be monitored by Coast Guard aircraft and cutters.
